title: How often should you really change your oil?
excerpt: The old 3,000-mile rule is long gone for most cars. Here's how to work out the right interval for yours.
content:
Most modern cars on synthetic oil can go 5,000 to 7,500 miles between changes, and some much further. Changing it too often wastes money; too rarely wears the engine out.

Start with your service book

Your maker sets the interval for your engine. Many cars also have an oil life monitor on the dash that works it out from how you drive.

Short trips count double

Lots of short trips in cold weather never let the oil warm up fully. If that's your driving, use the 'severe' schedule in the book.

Check the level every month

Pull the dipstick with the engine cold and the car level. If it's near the low mark between changes, tell us: some engines burn a little oil, some have a leak.

Use the right oil

The grade (like 0W-20) is printed on the oil cap or in the book. The wrong one can affect your warranty.

title: Five signs your brakes need attention
excerpt: Brakes wear slowly, so problems are easy to miss. These are the signs worth acting on.
content:
Brakes are the most important safety system on your car, and they almost always warn you before they fail.

Squealing

A high squeal when you brake is usually the pad wear indicator. Book a check in the next few weeks.

Grinding

Grinding means the pads are worn through and metal is on metal. Stop driving as much as you can and come in now.

A soft or sinking pedal

If the pedal feels spongy or sinks to the floor, there may be air or a leak in the system. Don't drive it: call us.

Pulling to one side

A car that pulls when you brake can have a sticking caliper or uneven pads.

Shaking through the wheel

Vibration when braking from speed often means warped rotors. Our brake check is free, with photos of what we find.

title: When to replace your tires (the penny test and more)
excerpt: Tread depth, age and wear patterns all tell you something. Here's how to read them in two minutes.
content:
Worn tires take much longer to stop in the wet. Checking them takes two minutes and a coin.

Do the penny test

Put a penny into the tread with Lincoln's head pointing down. If you can see the top of his head, the tread is below 2/32 of an inch and the tires need replacing now.

Check the age

The last four digits of the DOT code on the sidewall are the week and year it was made. Over six years old, replace them even if the tread looks fine.

Look at how they wear

Wear on both edges means low pressure; wear in the middle means too much. Wear on one edge usually means the alignment is out.

Check the pressure monthly

The right pressure is on a sticker inside the driver's door, not on the tire. Check when the tires are cold.

title: Get your car battery ready for an Idaho winter
excerpt: Cold mornings are when weak batteries give up. A free test in the fall saves a call for a jump start in January.
content:
A battery loses about a third of its power at freezing and more below. A battery that was fine in October can leave you stuck on the first cold morning.

Know its age

Most batteries last three to five years here. Look for a date sticker on the top.

Watch for slow starts

If the engine turns over slowly, or the lights dim when you start, the battery or charging system is getting weak.

Keep the terminals clean

White or green crust on the terminals stops the battery charging properly. We clean them free with any test.

Get it tested before winter

Our test checks the battery, the starter and the alternator together, free, in about ten minutes.
